Professor Gilboa held faculty posts at Harvard and Tel Aviv University in Israel, and was a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington. In 2001, he received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Science for his work on probability and economics, including his development of a theory called subjective expected utility theory. The theory holds that people who are engaging in economic decisions are best described not as seeking objective utility, or well-being, but rather as having complex emotional responses to risk that are difficult to quantify but that help determine how they act. In economic terms, the theory holds that decisions are made not just on the basis of expected gain but also influenced by pleasure and pain and other factors that are hard to measure.
